Stock Theft / Slicing

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Brutal scenes of animals slaughtered alive on farms and sold for their meat has left farmers in a state of shock. Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
Stock theft cost South Africa billions of rand every year. In 2018, 29 000 cases of stock theft was registered. Every day 178 cattle, 249 sheep and 115 goats are stolen in the country. In the Freestate alone the farming communities have suffered losses on average of ten million rand per month.

But it goes beyond the financial loss to the traumatic impact on the farmer when faced with the carnage left behind after the slaughtering. Some farmers have described it as senseless killing, maiming animals for their body parts and leaving them to die.


Summary:
As farmers increased their security and branding of their stock, perpetrators have turned to a different modus operandi of stock theft to avoid tracing and tracking of animals. The method involves moving onto the farms at night with groups of men known as “kappers.” Armed with sticks and pangas they work swiftly hacking off the animals’ back Achilles tendons so the cattle can’t walk. The animal is then sliced alive taking only the shoulder and hindquarter. At the scene pregnant cows lie butchered with the unborn fetus next to the carcass and in some instances calves are standing next to the cow waiting to be fed. With sheep and goats, they are chased into a corner and then tied by the feet before they are beheaded.

An informer has described how the gangs operate: A taxi will drop off the “Kappers” at the target farm where they will be picked up again when the job is done. A second vehicle will collect the meat. This is often a minibus or taxi with the seats removed. Meat is placed on order for big events like funerals or weddings and raids happen mostly before a weekend. Tracing the meat is virtually impossible as the perpetrators leave the body parts like the eartags behind that contain farmer’s identification.


Further information:
It was on a Saturday morning the 1st of June 2019 on a farm in the Kokstad area that Petrus Skosana found the shed broken into and the goats missing. He immediately alerted his employer, Gert van Aswegen about the situation and together they went looking for the animals. They got word from the next door neighbouring farm that his fence was cut and a few goats were seen on the property. At the scene 17 goats were found, severely mutilated and only a few still alive. The rest were presumably stolen.

Petrus described the scene as “very bad for the goats. Who can do such a thing.” Most of the goats were either pregnant or had young kid goats. The young kids were clobbed on the head and left behind. One survived.

This is the second incident of stock theft on van Aswegen’s farm in the last 3 months. “I cannot absorb the loss. They have wiped me out and caused suffering for my animals,” he says.

Forty kilometres from van Aswegen’s farm cattle breeder Marius Fouche accounts the horrific story of the morning he came across his mutilated animals. Their shins cut, some were still trying to hobble away on their knees; a calf rubs stands alone in the distance without his mother and mutilated body parts are strewn across the veld in a sea of red. “I cried like a child. The one cow’s tongue was bitten in half as she must have suffered.”

Fouche reported five incidents of stock theft in that year losing 60 cattle in total. Every case was reported to the police but “nothing came of it. It is so frustrating that the police are not able to find out who did it,” he says.

“I do the detective work for the police, even get the one of the gang leaders, and what happens? A case that should have been a conviction gets thrown out of court,” says Adolf Greeff, another farmer of the Parys region. Greeff tells us that there is frustration amongst the farmers: “we all know the police do not have enough manpower or vehicles to do the job properly.”

Greeff lost 32 cattle worth R600 000 in the last 12 months alone to the ‘kapperbende.’ “The worst is they slice chunks off the animal while still alive and they have no respect. Calves are left without a mother. It is cruel. That is all I can say.”

“Stock theft happens across borders and we have found that often meet stolen here in Parys makes its way to areas in Gauteng” says Sarel van der Watt. A farmer by trade, van der Watt has put in four years of extensive work in community policing. Through the reporting mechanism on the farming community networking channels stock thefts are reported and images of brand marks is spread through the WhatsApp group to look out for stolen stock. “The problem is they leave the identification marks of the animals behind and unless DNA samples are taken of the meat itself and we have a lead of where the meat is sold to try and match the sample, we are not able to catch the perpetrators”, says van der Watt.

Van der Watt is the representative for the Stock Theft Prevention Forum on interprovincial level and he says the police lacks specialised training and there is simply not enough manpower and vehicles to cover the vast rural areas where stock theft occurs. On national level, he reports to Willie Clack, the chairman of the Stock Theft Prevention Forum who compiles the statistics and analysis of the economic impact and changing modus operandi of stock theft.

The National Stock Theft Prevention Forum (NSTPF) works with crime prevention groups across the country and it has become clear that the modus operandi of the livestock perpetrators have changed over the last four years; the brutality of the crime has called for specialised training and operations to combat this form of crime and bring perpetrators to book, says Clack.

The South African Police Service has rolled out a plan to implement a joint Rural Safety Plan which they hope will address the crime in the rural community in an integrated manner, says Brigadier Kgopodithata, the National Head for SAPS Stock Theft and Endangrd Species Detective Services. SAPS have realised that conventional and normal policing practices are not effective in addressing stock theft and that a coordinated approach with Crime Intelligence, Organised Crime, Stock Theft Units, Visible Policing, Hawks and NPA is necessary to fight stock theft.

Our story: We uncover the brutal face of stock theft as criminals have resorted to the maiming of animals leaving shocking scenes behind that has traumatised farmers beyond words. We hear from an informer how the “Kapperbende” operate and the role of each player in this organised crime. We hear the stories from the farmers and ask the police why they have not been able to get on top of this brutal form of stock theft that has escalated out of control.

Press Release:


Livestock Butchers
Cattle, sheep and goat farmers lose billions every year to marauding stock thieves. Long used to defending their farms against stock theft, farmers now have to implement even more extraordinary measures to protect their livestock from having prime cuts of meat butchered on the farms, while the animals are still alive. Carte Blanche investigates this shifting, growing crime trend and the levels of animal cruelty that leaves behind grotesque carcasses, causing trauma for farmers and their employees.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


Script: Stock Theft
Duration: 10 minutes

V/O Stock theft costs South Africa billions of rands annually. In 2018, 29 000 cases of stock theft were registered. Every day 178 cattle, 249 sheep and 115 goats are stolen in the country. In the Free State alone, farming communities suffer losses on average of R10 million rands per month.

Up audio: Gert walking in veld with Petrus and the goats

V/O Gert van Aswegen is a farmer in the Kroonstad district; one of the hotspots targeted by stock thieves. Van Aswegen has had two incidents in the last three months that nearly wiped him out. It’s not only about financial loss, but it’s about the traumatic impact on a farming community when they realise their animals were butchered alive. Van Aswegen’s helper, Petrus Skosana, was first on the scene.

Petrus Skosana: (Sesotho translation) Four were butchered and just lying there.

Link: It was on a Saturday morning on the first of June when Petrus came here and found that this door broken open and some of the goats had gone missing. He then immediately phoned his employer Gert van Aswegen.

V/O Van Aswegen got word from his next-door neighbour that his fence had been cut and a few goats were on the neighbouring farm. At the scene they found 17 goats severely mutilated for their meat; a few were barely still alive.

Macrfarlane Moleli: When you came here, what did you find?

Petrus Skosana: Farmworker (Sesotho translation) About 600meters from the gate somewhere down there, we found two goats, very small ones. They were beaten brutally and mercilessly. They were bleeding both in the nose and mouth, one goat had died of cold.

Macfarlane Moleli: Hoe was dit vir jou om jou diere so te sien?

Gert van Aswegen: Farmer - Dis verskriklik.(It is terrible) Van hulle was vier groot oie wat geslag was (Amongst them were four big ewes that were slaughtered); koppe afgesny maar die vleis is nie verwyder nie (heads were cut off but the meat was not removed). So hulle het net eenvoudig daar gele en dood gebloei.(So the animals simply bled to death).

V/O About 100km from Van Aswegen’s farm, a cattle breeder near Parys in North West, fell victim. Marius Fouche took this video on his cellphone the morning after his livestock were slaughtered.

Up audio cellphone video (Translation): Hier le twee beeste. (Here are two dead cattle). Ek het nou al twee afgeneem (I have filmed two already.)

Marius Fouche: Farmer - As jy daar ry en sien die drade is geknip (When you drive and see the fence is cut,) dan voel dit soos n aardbewing wat deur jou gaan. (it feels like an earthquake going through you) en as jy in die veld ingaan en jy kom op die tonele af (If you go into the veld and come across the scene,) daar is nie woorde daarvoor nie. (there are no words to describe it.) Jy huil soos n kind.(You cry like a child)

UP cellphone: (Translation): Hulle sit al die eiers onderstebo. (They put all the udders upside down.) Dis n teken van hulle (It is a sign they were there.)

V/O Fouche lost 60 cattle in one year to stock theft. The animals were butchered alive for their meat.

Marius Fouche; Die laaste keer wat hulle gekap het was daar 9 wat daar gele het. (The last time they butchered, there were 9 animals lying there.) Jy kom nooit daaroor nie want die mense word nie gevang nie. (You never get over it because the people are not being caught.)

V/O Rural areas are particularly difficult to control as criminals use the back roads to make a quick getaway.

Link: So, this is one of the hotspot roads where the road link the Free State, North West and Gauteng. As you can see it is a vast track of land and a bit difficult for the police to patrol but it is also a double edged sword for the farmer: if you take your animals and you put them in a kraal it is easier for the criminals to get to them, if you let them roam free, they cut the fence. So how do you actually stop them?

V/O Adolf Greeff farms east of Parys in the Free State where his cattle graze in a camp near the N1 highway leading to Gauteng. He has lost 32 cattle worth R600 000 in one year.

Macfarlane Moleli: Do you have an idea in terms of the modus operandi? How do they stop them, I mean these are huge animals. How do they start getting the meat from them?

Adolf Greeff: Hulle jaag die koeie dan na n hoek toe in n kamp. (They chase the cows into a corner in a camp,) Dan het hulle byle en pangas dan kap hulle die sening (then they chop the shins with pangas and axes.) en sodra die sening gekap is dan gooi hulle die koei net om; hy is nog lewendig, (As soon as they’ve cut the shin they throw the cow down; it is still alive it can’t do anything;) hulle sny die twee boude en blaaie af lewendig. (they slice the hind quarters and shoulders while it is still alive).

UP cellphone video

V/O The most recent incident was in April this year where cows with week-old calves were slaughtered.

Adolf Greeff: En daai klein kalfie gaan staan en hy druk sy ma se kop en hy suig daar aan die doie koei se speen (And that small calf stand and push on his mother’s head and suck on the dead cow’s udder,) en dit is nogal hartseer as jy dit sien. (and that is very sad to see.)

V/O Tracing the stolen meat is virtually impossible as thieves simply leave the body part containing the identification tag, like on this ear, behind.

Adolf Greeff: Op al die slagtingstonele sny hulle die oor af (At all the scenes of slaughtering they cut the ear off.) So waar jy ook al die vleis gaan kry as is die bewys is weg. (So wherever you might find the meat you will not find the proof.)

V/O This informer told us the meat is sold next to informal settlements and to the butchers, who buy it cheaply.

Macfarlane Moleli: What is happening to all this meat? Where is it going?

Informer: We have a lot of restaurants in town. So the demand for the goats from those restaurants is high and they have lots of loopholes. Nobody is questioning them as far as the safety is concerned where the get the meat from.

Macfarlane Moleli: How do these guys actually operate? What do they do?

Informer: You will find all sorts of things, pangas, knives. Like I told you they don’t skin: cut it into pieces that are manageable portions just to be able to pick it up and put it into a car. Even the type of cars that they load on. Maybe it will be a Kombi.

Macfarlane Moleli: Why are they getting from those front and back quarters?

Informer I don’t even think they get half of what the cow is worth. In Lenasia south they were selling the cow’s hindquarter for R250.

Macfarlane Moleli: That is almost nothing

Informer: Almost nothing.

Up audio: Sarel van der Watt traveling in vehicle

V/O Sarel van der Watt is a foot soldier and a representative of the Interprovincial Stock Theft Prevention Forum. He reports incidents to a WhatsApp group as they happen.

Up driving sound

V/O Through the reporting mechanism of the community network channels, farmers are notified of incidents. All stats are reported to Willie Clack of The National Stock Theft Prevention Forum which works with crime prevention groups to investigate the modus operandi of the thieves and identify hotspots.

Willie Clack: Chairman National Livestock Prevention Forum: We currently have 80% under reporting of livestock theft in South Africa. All we are asking for the whole community to get involved. We cannot only rely on the police to stop stock theft. We need to do it collectively as a community otherwise we will not stop this problem.

V/O Farm-related crime happens across borders. Tonight’s operation is a joint safety cross border operation between the Free State, North West and Gauteng.

Up audio: Tonight, we have identified key routes where we must focus at that must be closed. If there is a criminal who plan to go out tonight he chose the wrong date and the wrong time. So, the theme is rural safety, blue, white light operation.

V/O The aim is to pool resources between government, business and the farming community to work together. Piet Kemp is the safety coordinator for Free State Agriculture and the link between the farmers, the local community and the police.

Piet Kemp: You drive out and you are doing patrol can easily do 200km on an evening so you can understand that because of the area and so many roads it is impossible to cover all the roads in a complete area in one night so you need a huge lot of manpower to do that.

Up audio: ..daaikant is waar n ou met skaapvleis of beesvleis.. Hier kan gesteelde voertuie wees.

Piet Kemp: These stop and search points that we have here helps us while some of the community patrollers and the farmers are patrolling the internal roads to make sure there is no activity on the inside.

Up audio: There is a problem on his farm.

V/O One farmer reports there’s movement on his land, but after some of the patrollers make a sweep of his property, they report all is in order - at least for tonight.

Up natural sound

V/O There are 90 stock theft units in South Africa, but with the increase of livestock butchering in certain hotspots, additional resources have been assembled. Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata is the Section Head.

Macfarlane Moleli: Brigadier, before stock theft use to be about stealing of animals where they were just being taken but now you are seeing a different trend where you will find they are just being butchered there on the farm.

Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: Section Head: Stock Theft and Endangered Species: After we discovered it is now becoming rife we embarked on establishing what we call stock theft information centers. In other word we created some sort of relationship between ourselves and the members of the community.

Mac: Can you call what is happening a syndicate?

Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: I would not say it is a syndicate. We have cases are now running before court where an individual was arrested. Remember sometimes our people are slaughtering these animals because they don’t have any other way of living.

Macfarlane Moleli: Brigadier the issue of poverty is one but here we are dealing with 15 animals slaughtered alive where a market is ready for it so it is a crime versus an issue of hunger.

Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: Most of the time we are also engaging the NSPCA and among the charges that we are putting against whoever is arrested it will be cruelty to animal and contravention of meat safety act and then again that individual can also be charged for contravening stock theft act.

V/O. Stock theft has increased by 6.5% over the last year. The impact on every farmer and their employees who depend on their animals for their livelihood is worrying.

Marius Fouche: Dit is n groot kopseer en die gevalle wat die polisie saamwerk het ons baie sukses gehad. (It is a big headache, and the cases where the police has worked with us we have had success.) Maar die hele probleem is as die mense gearresteer word, hulle word nie gevonnis nie. (But the whole problem is that when the people are arrested, they are not being sentenced).

V/O Fouche has increased his security at a huge additional monthly expense.

Marius Fouche: In die nagte, ons beeste loop versprei, dan gaan die alarms af op een plaas, (At night our cattle are widespread; an alarm goes off on one farm,) dan op n ander plaas. (then on another farm.) Jy slaap ook nie. (You don’t sleep.) Jy werk bedags. Dit is n groot impak. (You work during the day. It is a big impact.)

V/O Van Aswegen is selling his remaining goats to avoid further losses.

Piet van Aswegen: Op hierdie stadium ly ons net aan verlies. (At this point we are only losing money.) Ons kan nie vorentoe gaan nie met al die skade wat ons ly. (We cannot carry on with all the loss we are experiencing).

V/O Greeff has been a farmer for 20 years and faced many challenges, but nothing compares to the trauma he’s undergone in the last year.

Adolf Greeff: Dit gaan nie net oor geld nie. (It is not only the money that is important) N ou is lief vir jou diere (One loves your animals) Ek ken daai koei, ek weet dit is haar kalf. (I know that cow; I know that is her calf) Daai ou koei was een van my eerste koeie, dis haar vers. Nou is sy gekap. (That old cow was one of my first cows; that is her calf. Now she is butchered) Dit maak jou hartseer. Dis nie lekker nie. (It makes you sad. It is not nice).

Sunday promo:
Stock theft has long threatened farming. Now, the crime displays new levels of cruelty where thieves dismember animals while they are still alive. How will farmers get on top of this?

Promo 1:
Long used to defending their farms against livestock thieves, farmers are now faced with violent acts of mutilation, where their animals are butchered alive for their meat - a sadistic crime spinning out of control.

Promo 2:
Livestock mutilation –a crime where stock thieves butcher animals alive for their meat. How are farmers coping with the trauma when faced with the shocking scene of those body parts left behind?

Promo 3:
Stock theft has long threatened farming, but now thieves have taken to butchering animals in the field – hacking off body parts sold as meat, and leaving the carcasses for the devastated farmer to find.

SAPS have realised that conventional and normal policing practices are not effective in addressing stock theft and that a coordinated approach with Crime Intelligence, Organised Crime, Stock Theft Units, Visible Policing, Hawks and NPA is necessary to fight stock theft. Our story: We uncover the brutal face of stock theft as criminals have resorted to the maiming of animals leaving shocking scenes behind that has traumatised farmers beyond words. We hear from an informer how the “Kapperbende” operate and the role of each player in this organised crime. We hear the stories from the farmers and ask the police why they have not been able to get on top of this brutal form of stock theft that has escalated out of control. Long used to defending their farms against stock theft, farmers now have to implement even more extraordinary measures to protect their livestock from having prime cuts of meat butchered on the farms, while the animals are still alive. Carte Blanche investigates this shifting, growing crime trend and the levels of animal cruelty that leaves behind grotesque carcasses, causing trauma for farmers and their employees. Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Script: Script: Stock Theft Duration: 10 minutes V/O Stock theft costs South Africa billions of rands annually. In 2018, 29 000 cases of stock theft were registered. Every day 178 cattle, 249 sheep and 115 goats are stolen in the country. In the Free State alone, farming communities suffer losses on average of R10 million rands per month. Up audio: Gert walking in veld with Petrus and the goats V/O Gert van Aswegen is a farmer in the Kroonstad district; one of the hotspots targeted by stock thieves. Van Aswegen has had two incidents in the last three months that nearly wiped him out. It’s not only about financial loss, but it’s about the traumatic impact on a farming community when they realise their animals were butchered alive. Van Aswegen’s helper, Petrus Skosana, was first on the scene. Petrus Skosana: (Sesotho translation) Four were butchered and just lying there. Link: It was on a Saturday morning on the first of June when Petrus came here and found that this door broken open and some of the goats had gone missing. He then immediately phoned his employer Gert van Aswegen. V/O Van Aswegen got word from his next-door neighbour that his fence had been cut and a few goats were on the neighbouring farm. At the scene they found 17 goats severely mutilated for their meat; a few were barely still alive. Macrfarlane Moleli: When you came here, what did you find? Petrus Skosana: Farmworker (Sesotho translation) About 600meters from the gate somewhere down there, we found two goats, very small ones. They were beaten brutally and mercilessly. They were bleeding both in the nose and mouth, one goat had died of cold. Macfarlane Moleli: Hoe was dit vir jou om jou diere so te sien? Gert van Aswegen: Farmer - Dis verskriklik.(It is terrible) Van hulle was vier groot oie wat geslag was (Amongst them were four big ewes that were slaughtered); koppe afgesny maar die vleis is nie verwyder nie (heads were cut off but the meat was not removed). So hulle het net eenvoudig daar gele en dood gebloei.(So the animals simply bled to death). V/O About 100km from Van Aswegen’s farm, a cattle breeder near Parys in North West, fell victim. Marius Fouche took this video on his cellphone the morning after his livestock were slaughtered. Up audio cellphone video (Translation): Hier le twee beeste. (Here are two dead cattle). Ek het nou al twee afgeneem (I have filmed two already.) Marius Fouche: Farmer - As jy daar ry en sien die drade is geknip (When you drive and see the fence is cut,) dan voel dit soos n aardbewing wat deur jou gaan. (it feels like an earthquake going through you) en as jy in die veld ingaan en jy kom op die tonele af (If you go into the veld and come across the scene,) daar is nie woorde daarvoor nie. (there are no words to describe it.) Jy huil soos n kind.(You cry like a child) UP cellphone: (Translation): Hulle sit al die eiers onderstebo. (They put all the udders upside down.) Dis n teken van hulle (It is a sign they were there.) V/O Fouche lost 60 cattle in one year to stock theft. The animals were butchered alive for their meat. Marius Fouche; Die laaste keer wat hulle gekap het was daar 9 wat daar gele het. (The last time they butchered, there were 9 animals lying there.) Jy kom nooit daaroor nie want die mense word nie gevang nie. (You never get over it because the people are not being caught.) V/O Rural areas are particularly difficult to control as criminals use the back roads to make a quick getaway. Link: So, this is one of the hotspot roads where the road link the Free State, North West and Gauteng. As you can see it is a vast track of land and a bit difficult for the police to patrol but it is also a double edged sword for the farmer: if you take your animals and you put them in a kraal it is easier for the criminals to get to them, if you let them roam free, they cut the fence. So how do you actually stop them? V/O Adolf Greeff farms east of Parys in the Free State where his cattle graze in a camp near the N1 highway leading to Gauteng. He has lost 32 cattle worth R600 000 in one year. Macfarlane Moleli: Do you have an idea in terms of the modus operandi? How do they stop them, I mean these are huge animals. How do they start getting the meat from them? Adolf Greeff: Hulle jaag die koeie dan na n hoek toe in n kamp. (They chase the cows into a corner in a camp,) Dan het hulle byle en pangas dan kap hulle die sening (then they chop the shins with pangas and axes.) en sodra die sening gekap is dan gooi hulle die koei net om; hy is nog lewendig, (As soon as they’ve cut the shin they throw the cow down; it is still alive it can’t do anything;) hulle sny die twee boude en blaaie af lewendig. (they slice the hind quarters and shoulders while it is still alive). UP cellphone video V/O The most recent incident was in April this year where cows with week-old calves were slaughtered. Adolf Greeff: En daai klein kalfie gaan staan en hy druk sy ma se kop en hy suig daar aan die doie koei se speen (And that small calf stand and push on his mother’s head and suck on the dead cow’s udder,) en dit is nogal hartseer as jy dit sien. (and that is very sad to see.) V/O Tracing the stolen meat is virtually impossible as thieves simply leave the body part containing the identification tag, like on this ear, behind. Adolf Greeff: Op al die slagtingstonele sny hulle die oor af (At all the scenes of slaughtering they cut the ear off.) So waar jy ook al die vleis gaan kry as is die bewys is weg. (So wherever you might find the meat you will not find the proof.) V/O This informer told us the meat is sold next to informal settlements and to the butchers, who buy it cheaply. Macfarlane Moleli: What is happening to all this meat? Where is it going? Informer: We have a lot of restaurants in town. So the demand for the goats from those restaurants is high and they have lots of loopholes. Nobody is questioning them as far as the safety is concerned where the get the meat from. Macfarlane Moleli: How do these guys actually operate? What do they do? Informer: You will find all sorts of things, pangas, knives. Like I told you they don’t skin: cut it into pieces that are manageable portions just to be able to pick it up and put it into a car. Even the type of cars that they load on. Maybe it will be a Kombi. Macfarlane Moleli: Why are they getting from those front and back quarters? Informer I don’t even think they get half of what the cow is worth. In Lenasia south they were selling the cow’s hindquarter for R250. Macfarlane Moleli: That is almost nothing Informer: Almost nothing. Up audio: Sarel van der Watt traveling in vehicle V/O Sarel van der Watt is a foot soldier and a representative of the Interprovincial Stock Theft Prevention Forum. He reports incidents to a WhatsApp group as they happen. Up driving sound V/O Through the reporting mechanism of the community network channels, farmers are notified of incidents. All stats are reported to Willie Clack of The National Stock Theft Prevention Forum which works with crime prevention groups to investigate the modus operandi of the thieves and identify hotspots. Willie Clack: Chairman National Livestock Prevention Forum: We currently have 80% under reporting of livestock theft in South Africa. All we are asking for the whole community to get involved. We cannot only rely on the police to stop stock theft. We need to do it collectively as a community otherwise we will not stop this problem. V/O Farm-related crime happens across borders. Tonight’s operation is a joint safety cross border operation between the Free State, North West and Gauteng. Up audio: Tonight, we have identified key routes where we must focus at that must be closed. If there is a criminal who plan to go out tonight he chose the wrong date and the wrong time. So, the theme is rural safety, blue, white light operation. V/O The aim is to pool resources between government, business and the farming community to work together. Piet Kemp is the safety coordinator for Free State Agriculture and the link between the farmers, the local community and the police. Piet Kemp: You drive out and you are doing patrol can easily do 200km on an evening so you can understand that because of the area and so many roads it is impossible to cover all the roads in a complete area in one night so you need a huge lot of manpower to do that. Up audio: ..daaikant is waar n ou met skaapvleis of beesvleis.. Hier kan gesteelde voertuie wees. Piet Kemp: These stop and search points that we have here helps us while some of the community patrollers and the farmers are patrolling the internal roads to make sure there is no activity on the inside. Up audio: There is a problem on his farm. V/O One farmer reports there’s movement on his land, but after some of the patrollers make a sweep of his property, they report all is in order - at least for tonight. Up natural sound V/O There are 90 stock theft units in South Africa, but with the increase of livestock butchering in certain hotspots, additional resources have been assembled. Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata is the Section Head. Macfarlane Moleli: Brigadier, before stock theft use to be about stealing of animals where they were just being taken but now you are seeing a different trend where you will find they are just being butchered there on the farm. Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: Section Head: Stock Theft and Endangered Species: After we discovered it is now becoming rife we embarked on establishing what we call stock theft information centers. In other word we created some sort of relationship between ourselves and the members of the community. Mac: Can you call what is happening a syndicate? Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: I would not say it is a syndicate. We have cases are now running before court where an individual was arrested. Remember sometimes our people are slaughtering these animals because they don’t have any other way of living. Macfarlane Moleli: Brigadier the issue of poverty is one but here we are dealing with 15 animals slaughtered alive where a market is ready for it so it is a crime versus an issue of hunger. Brigadier OJ Kgopodithata: Most of the time we are also engaging the NSPCA and among the charges that we are putting against whoever is arrested it will be cruelty to animal and contravention of meat safety act and then again that individual can also be charged for contravening stock theft act. V/O. Stock theft has increased by 6.5% over the last year. The impact on every farmer and their employees who depend on their animals for their livelihood is worrying. Marius Fouche: Dit is n groot kopseer en die gevalle wat die polisie saamwerk het ons baie sukses gehad. (It is a big headache, and the cases where the police has worked with us we have had success.) Maar die hele probleem is as die mense gearresteer word, hulle word nie gevonnis nie. (But the whole problem is that when the people are arrested, they are not being sentenced). V/O Fouche has increased his security at a huge additional monthly expense. Marius Fouche: In die nagte, ons beeste loop versprei, dan gaan die alarms af op een plaas, (At night our cattle are widespread; an alarm goes off on one farm,) dan op n ander plaas. (then on another farm.) Jy slaap ook nie. (You don’t sleep.) Jy werk bedags. Dit is n groot impak. (You work during the day. It is a big impact.) V/O Van Aswegen is selling his remaining goats to avoid further losses. Piet van Aswegen: Op hierdie stadium ly ons net aan verlies. (At this point we are only losing money.) Ons kan nie vorentoe gaan nie met al die skade wat ons ly. (We cannot carry on with all the loss we are experiencing). V/O Greeff has been a farmer for 20 years and faced many challenges, but nothing compares to the trauma he’s undergone in the last year. Adolf Greeff: Dit gaan nie net oor geld nie. (It is not only the money that is important) N ou is lief vir jou diere (One loves your animals) Ek ken daai koei, ek weet dit is haar kalf. (I know that cow; I know that is her calf) Daai ou koei was een van my eerste koeie, dis haar vers. Nou is sy gekap. (That old cow was one of my first cows; that is her calf. Now she is butchered) Dit maak jou hartseer. Dis nie lekker nie. (It makes you sad. It is not nice). ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Sunday promo: Stock theft has long threatened farming. Now, the crime displays new levels of cruelty where thieves dismember animals while they are still alive. How will farmers get on top of this? Promo 1: Long used to defending their farms against livestock thieves, farmers are now faced with violent acts of mutilation, where their animals are butchered alive for their meat - a sadistic crime spinning out of control. Promo 2: Livestock mutilation –a crime where stock thieves butcher animals alive for their meat. How are farmers coping with the trauma when faced with the shocking scene of those body parts left behind? Promo 3: Stock theft has long threatened farming, but now thieves have taken to butchering animals in the field – hacking off body parts sold as meat, and leaving the carcasses for the devastated farmer to find. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Brutal scenes of animals slaughtered alive on farms and sold for their meat has left farmers in a state of shock. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Stock theft cost South Africa billions of rand every year. In 2018, 29 000 cases of stock theft was registered. Every day 178 cattle, 249 sheep and 115 goats are stolen in the country. In the Freestate alone the farming communities have suffered losses on average of ten million rand per month. But it goes beyond the financial loss to the traumatic impact on the farmer when faced with the carnage left behind after the slaughtering. Some farmers have described it as senseless killing, maiming animals for their body parts and leaving them to die.
metadata.Summary: As farmers increased their security and branding of their stock, perpetrators have turned to a different modus operandi of stock theft to avoid tracing and tracking of animals. The method involves moving onto the farms at night with groups of men known as “kappers.” Armed with sticks and pangas they work swiftly hacking off the animals’ back Achilles tendons so the cattle can’t walk. The animal is then sliced alive taking only the shoulder and hindquarter. At the scene pregnant cows lie butchered with the unborn fetus next to the carcass and in some instances calves are standing next to the cow waiting to be fed. With sheep and goats, they are chased into a corner and then tied by the feet before they are beheaded. An informer has described how the gangs operate: A taxi will drop off the “Kappers” at the target farm where they will be picked up again when the job is done. A second vehicle will collect the meat. This is often a minibus or taxi with the seats removed. Meat is placed on order for big events like funerals or weddings and raids happen mostly before a weekend. Tracing the meat is virtually impossible as the perpetrators leave the body parts like the eartags behind that contain farmer’s identification.
metadata.Further information: It was on a Saturday morning the 1st of June 2019 on a farm in the Kokstad area that Petrus Skosana found the shed broken into and the goats missing. He immediately alerted his employer, Gert van Aswegen about the situation and together they went looking for the animals. They got word from the next door neighbouring farm that his fence was cut and a few goats were seen on the property. At the scene 17 goats were found, severely mutilated and only a few still alive. The rest were presumably stolen. Petrus described the scene as “very bad for the goats. Who can do such a thing.” Most of the goats were either pregnant or had young kid goats. The young kids were clobbed on the head and left behind. One survived. This is the second incident of stock theft on van Aswegen’s farm in the last 3 months. “I cannot absorb the loss. They have wiped me out and caused suffering for my animals,” he says. Forty kilometres from van Aswegen’s farm cattle breeder Marius Fouche accounts the horrific story of the morning he came across his mutilated animals. Their shins cut, some were still trying to hobble away on their knees; a calf rubs stands alone in the distance without his mother and mutilated body parts are strewn across the veld in a sea of red. “I cried like a child. The one cow’s tongue was bitten in half as she must have suffered.” Fouche reported five incidents of stock theft in that year losing 60 cattle in total. Every case was reported to the police but “nothing came of it. It is so frustrating that the police are not able to find out who did it,” he says. “I do the detective work for the police, even get the one of the gang leaders, and what happens? A case that should have been a conviction gets thrown out of court,” says Adolf Greeff, another farmer of the Parys region. Greeff tells us that there is frustration amongst the farmers: “we all know the police do not have enough manpower or vehicles to do the job properly.” Greeff lost 32 cattle worth R600 000 in the last 12 months alone to the ‘kapperbende.’ “The worst is they slice chunks off the animal while still alive and they have no respect. Calves are left without a mother. It is cruel. That is all I can say.” “Stock theft happens across borders and we have found that often meet stolen here in Parys makes its way to areas in Gauteng” says Sarel van der Watt. A farmer by trade, van der Watt has put in four years of extensive work in community policing. Through the reporting mechanism on the farming community networking channels stock thefts are reported and images of brand marks is spread through the WhatsApp group to look out for stolen stock. “The problem is they leave the identification marks of the animals behind and unless DNA samples are taken of the meat itself and we have a lead of where the meat is sold to try and match the sample, we are not able to catch the perpetrators”, says van der Watt. Van der Watt is the representative for the Stock Theft Prevention Forum on interprovincial level and he says the police lacks specialised training and there is simply not enough manpower and vehicles to cover the vast rural areas where stock theft occurs. On national level, he reports to Willie Clack, the chairman of the Stock Theft Prevention Forum who compiles the statistics and analysis of the economic impact and changing modus operandi of stock theft. The National Stock Theft Prevention Forum (NSTPF) works with crime prevention groups across the country and it has become clear that the modus operandi of the livestock perpetrators have changed over the last four years; the brutality of the crime has called for specialised training and operations to combat this form of crime and bring perpetrators to book, says Clack. The South African Police Service has rolled out a plan to implement a joint Rural Safety Plan which they hope will address the crime in the rural community in an integrated manner, says Brigadier Kgopodithata, the National Head for SAPS Stock Theft and Endangrd Species Detective Services. SAPS have realised that conventional and normal policing practices are not effective in addressing stock theft and that a coordinated approach with Crime Intelligence, Organised Crime, Stock Theft Units, Visible Policing, Hawks and NPA is necessary to fight stock theft. Our story: We uncover the brutal face of stock theft as criminals have resorted to the maiming of animals leaving shocking scenes behind that has traumatised farmers beyond words. We hear from an informer how the “Kapperbende” operate and the role of each player in this organised crime. We hear the stories from the farmers and ask the police why they have not been able to get on top of this brutal form of stock theft that has escalated out of control.
